newsitem.title: USA: Fundraiser Huang telephone calls reported. [CORRECTED 01:02 GMT 19/11]
newsitem.headline: Fundraiser Huang telephone calls reported. [CORRECTED 01:02 GMT 19/11]

text.p: Fundraiser John Huang, who solicited controversial Democratic campaign contributions from foreign interests, made 70 telephone calls to a bank controlled by his former Indonesian boss, a Republican House chairman, citing telephone records, said on Monday.

The telephone records "also reveal a pattern of calls to prominent Little Rock (Arkansas) entrepreneurs and lawyers with extensive financial interests in Asia," Representative Benjamin Gilman, chairman of the House International Relations Committee, said in a letter.

"Clearly this information is highly relevant to the allegations that surfaced late in the presidential campaign about questionable fundraising practices involving John Huang," Gilman, a New York Republican, said.

Huang was accused of soliciting questionable foreign contributions for the Democratic National Committee for recent election campaigns, including $250,000 from a South Korean company and $5,000 at a Buddhist temple fundraising event.

Gilman said telephone records showed Huang made the 70 calls to the Lippo Bank in Los Angeles, which is controlled by billionaire Indonesia businessman James Riady's family, while Huang worked for the Commerce Department (corrects from Justice Department).
Huang worked for Riady as a senior executive before becoming a Commerce Department official. He left that job to become a senior fundraiser for the Democratic National Committee.

A spokeswoman said earlier on Monday that the Democratic National Committee had laid off Huang, as part of a general reduction in staff not because of the allegations of soliciting questionable contributions.
Amy Weiss Tobe said Huang was among 50 DNC employees laid off on Friday as the election season wound down. She said the decision was not due to the controversy surrounding Huang.

"He was let go as part of the downsizing" at the committee after the Nov. 5 election, she said. Huang had already been relieved of his fundraising duties, but he continued to draw a salary from the party until last week.

Huang had been the DNC's finance vice chairman since December 1995 and raised $2.5 million for the party, much of it from the Asian-American community. But nearly $600,000 of this has been returned after questions were raised about the source of the money.
This included $250,000 that came from a Korean company rather than its U.S. subsidiary. It is illegal for foreign nationals to contribute to U.S. elections.

Questions about Democratic fundraising were an issue in the closing weeks of the presidential campaign and some analysts believe the controversy reduced President Bill Clinton's margin of victory over Republican Bob Dole.
